questions.title: Main product lines
questions.story: What product lines does AdventureWorks sell? List the categories and the sub-categories.
approach: Category names are in ADW_Dim_ProductCategory and sub-category names are in ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory.
There are 4 categories (Bikes, Accessories, Clothing and Components) and 37 sub-categories.
This is an exploration query with no condition. To see which sub-category belongs to which category, you need a JOIN (Lesson 3).

steps.title: Categories
steps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT ProductCategoryName
FROM ADW_Dim_ProductCategory

steps.title: Sub-categories
steps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT ProductSubCategoryName
FROM ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory

questions.title: Where the company operates
questions.story: Where does AdventureWorks operate? Return the territory, the country and the region group.
approach: Geography is in ADW_Dim_Territory.
There are 10 territories in 6 countries: US (5 territories), CA, FR, DE, AU and GB.
Group is a reserved word in T-SQL, so write it as [Group]. Note the territory IDs, because HW 9 uses them.

steps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT TerritoryName, CountryRegionCode, [Group]
FROM ADW_Dim_Territory

questions.title: Why customers buy
questions.story: Why do customers buy from AdventureWorks? List the purchase reasons.
approach: Purchase reasons are in ADW_Dim_Sales_Reason (column ReasonName).
There are 10 reasons, grouped into types such as Promotion, Marketing and Other.

steps.sql:
SELECT *
FROM ADW_Dim_Sales_Reason

questions.title: Wrongly priced products
questions.story: A colleague named Peter set the wrong price on some products that have already been sold. A wrong price means a unit price above 3,500. List the orders that contain these products, so the product team can review them.
approach: Sold products are in ADW_Sales_orders_detail, which has one row per product line.
The price is the UnitPrice column. It is on the detail table, not on the order header.
One order can have several expensive lines, so use DISTINCT.

steps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT SalesOrderID
FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail
WHERE UnitPrice > 3500

questions.title: Refund for customer 29641
questions.story: Customer 29641 called and wants a refund for the order shipped on 2013-06-06. Check the order value (SubTotal) so the customer service team can handle the ticket.
approach: The customer ID (CustomerID) and the ship date (ShipDate) are both in ADW_Sales_orders.
Write dates as yyyy-MM-dd.
Filter on the ship date, not the order date. This order was placed on 2013-05-30 and shipped on 2013-06-06.
Exactly one order should match.

steps.sql:
SELECT CustomerID, SalesOrderID, OrderDate, SubTotal
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
WHERE CustomerID = 29641 AND ShipDate = '2013-06-06'

questions.title: Cards ending in 9916
questions.story: The card partner reports that cards ending in 9916 are fraudulent. List the orders paid with these cards, so the risk team can review them.
questions.hint: The card number is in the CardNumber column of ADW_Dim_CreditCard. Work in two steps.
approach: Step 1: use pattern matching on CardNumber to find the CreditCardID of the cards ending in 9916 (3 cards).
Step 2: orders paid by card carry a CreditCardID in ADW_Sales_orders. Filter on the IDs from step 1 (4 orders).
Hard-coded IDs go stale. A subquery with IN does both steps in one query (Lesson 5).

steps.title: Step 1: find the cards ending in 9916
steps.sql:
SELECT *
FROM ADW_Dim_CreditCard
WHERE CardNumber LIKE '%9916'

steps.title: Step 2: find the orders paid with those cards
steps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT SalesOrderID, TotalDue, CreditCardID, CustomerID
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
WHERE CreditCardID IN ('166', '6177', '14469')

questions.title: Highest standard costs
questions.story: The Finance team is reviewing production costs. List the 10 products with the highest standard cost, and show the ratio of standard cost to list price for each.
approach: Standard cost (StandardCost) and list price (ListPrice) are both in ADW_Dim_Product.
Sort StandardCost from high to low and keep 10 rows. Add a ratio column: StandardCost / ListPrice.
Several products tie on cost at the 10th place, so only the cost column is checked. Add a second sort column to make the list stable.

steps.sql:
SELECT TOP 10 *, StandardCost/ListPrice*100 AS Standard_cost_per_listprice_ratio
FROM ADW_Dim_Product
ORDER BY StandardCost DESC

questions.note: rows tie on StandardCost at the 10th place, so only the cost column is compared

questions.title: Promotions for resellers
questions.story: Which promotions do we run for resellers? Return the special offer ID and its description.
approach: Promotions are in ADW_Dim_SpecialOffer. The Category column says who each offer is for.
Run SELECT DISTINCT Category first to see the exact values, then filter on Reseller.
There are 13 reseller offers.

steps.sql:
SELECT SpecialOfferID, Description
FROM ADW_Dim_SpecialOffer
WHERE Category = 'Reseller'

questions.title: Two customer groups in one query
questions.story:
The Customer Research team is studying customers in different regions. Find the customers who bought in 2012 and fit one of these two groups:
- Online buyers in Canada or France, with an order value of at least 1,000.
- Offline buyers in the US or Australia, with an order value between 600 and 1,000.
Return CustomerID, TerritoryID, ship date, order value and the online/offline flag.
questions.hint: Both groups must come back from one query.
approach: Look at ADW_Dim_Territory first and note the TerritoryID of Canada, France, the US (five territories) and Australia.
The 2012 filter applies to both groups, so it goes outside. Each group is its own bracket of AND conditions, and the two brackets are joined with OR.
Order value is TotalDue. OnlineOrderFlag is 1 for online and 0 for offline.
Test each group alone first. Without the outer brackets, AND binds before OR and the 2012 filter would apply to only one group.

steps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT CustomerID, TerritoryID, OnlineOrderFlag, TotalDue, ShipDate
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
WHERE (OrderDate BETWEEN '2012-01-01' AND '2012-12-31')
  AND (
        (TerritoryID IN (6,7) AND OnlineOrderFlag = 1 AND TotalDue >= 1000)
        OR
        (TerritoryID IN (1,2,3,4,5,9) AND OnlineOrderFlag = 0 AND TotalDue BETWEEN 600 AND 1000)
      )

questions.title: Online in Q4 2013 or offline in Q1 2012
questions.story: The Customer Research team wants to compare online and offline buyers. Find the customers who bought offline in Q1 2012, or online in Q4 2013. Return CustomerID, order year, order quarter and the online/offline flag.
approach: There are three ways to filter Q1: a date range, MONTH IN (1, 2, 3), or DATEPART(QUARTER, ...) = 1.
Watch the nested conditions when you join the two groups with OR.
A quarter number alone is not enough, because Q1 exists in every year. Always pair it with the year.

steps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT CustomerID, YEAR(OrderDate) AS OrderYear, DATEPART(QUARTER, OrderDate) AS OrderQuarter, OnlineOrderFlag
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
WHERE (OnlineOrderFlag = 0 AND DATEPART(QUARTER, OrderDate) = 1 AND YEAR(OrderDate) = 2012)
   OR (OnlineOrderFlag = 1 AND DATEPART(QUARTER, OrderDate) = 4 AND YEAR(OrderDate) = 2013)

questions.title: Won deals above list price
questions.story: List the deals won in 2017 whose closing value is higher than the list price of the product.
approach: Deals are in CRM_sales_pipeline. The list price is in CRM_products, so use a LEFT JOIN to keep every deal.
A won deal has deal_stage = 'Won'. Filter the close date on 2017.

Check the join. The pipeline writes one product as GTXPro and the product list writes GTX Pro. Those deals get a NULL price and drop out of the comparison without any error. Lesson 8 comes back to this.

steps.sql:
SELECT t1.*, t2.sales_price
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline t1
LEFT JOIN CRM_products t2 ON t1.product = t2.product
WHERE deal_stage = 'Won'
  AND t1.close_value > t2.sales_price
  AND YEAR(close_date) = 2017

questions.title: Regions that lost deals in Q1 2017
questions.story: Which regions had agents who lost deals in the first three months of 2017?
approach: Deals are in CRM_sales_pipeline. The region is in CRM_sales_teams, joined on sales_agent.
A lost deal has deal_stage = 'Lost', with a close date from 2017-01-01 to 2017-03-31.
Many deals share a region, so use DISTINCT.

steps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT t2.regional_office
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline t1
LEFT JOIN CRM_sales_teams t2 ON t1.sales_agent = t2.sales_agent
WHERE deal_stage = 'Lost'
  AND close_date BETWEEN '2017-01-01' AND '2017-03-31'

questions.title: Products sold to the marketing sector
questions.story: Which products were sold to companies in the marketing sector in won deals in 2017?
approach: The sector of each customer company is in CRM_Accounts, joined on account.
Run SELECT DISTINCT sector FROM CRM_Accounts first to see the exact spelling before you filter.
Filter on won deals closed in 2017 with sector = 'marketing'. Use DISTINCT on the product.

steps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT t1.product
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline t1
LEFT JOIN CRM_Accounts t2 ON t1.account = t2.account
WHERE deal_stage = 'Won'
  AND YEAR(close_date) = 2017
  AND sector = 'marketing'

questions.title: Sectors of the top 10 deals
questions.story: Which sectors do the 10 highest-value deals of all time belong to?
approach: Deal value is close_value in CRM_sales_pipeline. The sector comes from CRM_Accounts, as in the last question.
Take the won deals, sort by close_value from high to low and keep the top 10.
The answer is the list of distinct sectors in those 10 deals (6 sectors).

steps.title: Top 10 deals with their sector
steps.sql:
SELECT TOP 10 t1.*, t2.sector
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline t1
LEFT JOIN CRM_Accounts t2 ON t1.account = t2.account
WHERE deal_stage = 'Won'
ORDER BY close_value DESC

alts:
SELECT DISTINCT t2.sector
FROM (SELECT TOP 10 * FROM CRM_sales_pipeline WHERE deal_stage = 'Won' ORDER BY close_value DESC) t1
LEFT JOIN CRM_Accounts t2 ON t1.account = t2.account

questions.title: Fastest and slowest deals
questions.story: Which 10 deals closed fastest and which 10 closed slowest?
approach: Closing time = close_date minus engage_date. Use DATEDIFF in days.
Many deals share the same number of days, so the top 10 can differ between valid answers. Compare with the model output.
Only Won and Lost deals have a close date, so open deals are left out. Putting ORDER BY inside a UNION branch needs a wrapper query (Lesson 5 material).

steps.sql:
SELECT *, 'Shortest' AS type_
FROM (
    SELECT TOP 10 *, DATEDIFF(DAY, engage_date, close_date) AS close_deal_duration
    FROM CRM_sales_pipeline
    WHERE LOWER(deal_stage) IN ('won','lost')
    ORDER BY close_deal_duration ASC
) t1
UNION ALL
SELECT *, 'Longest' AS type_
FROM (
    SELECT TOP 10 *, DATEDIFF(DAY, engage_date, close_date) AS close_deal_duration
    FROM CRM_sales_pipeline
    WHERE LOWER(deal_stage) IN ('won','lost')
    ORDER BY close_deal_duration DESC
) t2

questions.title: Europe customers on Vista or SuperiorCard
questions.story: The Payment team is running a survey in Europe. List the customers who bought in Europe in Q3 2013 and paid with a Vista or SuperiorCard. Return the CustomerID and the card type.
questions.hint: When a question is only about orders, ADW_Sales_orders is the base table.
approach: Start from ADW_Sales_orders. Add the card type from ADW_Dim_CreditCard and the region group from ADW_Dim_Territory.
The join keys are CreditCardID and TerritoryID. The two CreditCardID columns have different data types, so CAST them to the same type before the JOIN.
INNER JOIN is fine here, because orders without a card should drop out.
Group is a reserved word, so write [Group] in brackets.

steps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT t1.CustomerID, t2.CardType
FROM ADW_Sales_orders t1
JOIN ADW_Dim_CreditCard t2
    ON CAST(t2.CreditCardID AS NVARCHAR) = CAST(t1.CreditCardID AS NVARCHAR)
JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory t3 ON t3.TerritoryID = t1.TerritoryID
WHERE [Group] = 'EUROPE'
  AND DATEPART(QUARTER, OrderDate) = 3
  AND YEAR(OrderDate) = 2013
  AND t2.CardType IN ('Vista', 'SuperiorCard')

questions.title: Black or Silver Mountain Bikes with cost 1,000 to 1,500
questions.story: The Product team wants a list of Mountain Bikes that are Black or Silver and have a standard cost between 1,000 and 1,500. Also show the ratio of standard cost to list price for each product.
approach: Products are in ADW_Dim_Product. The sub-category name is in ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory, one table away.
Filter the sub-category on 'Mountain Bikes', the colour on Black or Silver, and StandardCost with BETWEEN 1000 AND 1500.
The join keys have different data types, so CAST them to the same type.
There are 6 products. Their cost is about 54.6% of list price.

steps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT ProductID, ProductName, t2.ProductSubCategoryName, StandardCost, ListPrice,
       StandardCost/ListPrice AS cost_ratio
FROM ADW_Dim_Product t1
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory t2
    ON t1.ProductSubcategoryID = CAST(t2.ProductSubcategoryID AS VARCHAR)
WHERE t2.ProductSubCategoryName = 'Mountain Bikes'
  AND Color IN ('Black', 'Silver')
  AND StandardCost BETWEEN 1000 AND 1500

questions.title: Orders of the top 10 customers of 2011 and 2012
questions.story: The company wants to thank its biggest spenders of 2011 and 2012. Get every order (order ID, customer ID and total due) of the top 10 customers of each year.
questions.hint: The customer lists are in the tables ADW_Top_10_spending_cust_2011 and ADW_Top_10_spending_cust_2012.
approach: You only want the orders of these customers, so use INNER JOIN on CustomerID, once per year.
Combine the two years with UNION.
Extra: you can get the same rows with a LEFT JOIN and WHERE ... IS NOT NULL on the joined key, without swapping the tables.

steps.sql:
SELECT SalesOrderID, t1.CustomerID, TotalDue
FROM ADW_Top_10_spending_cust_2011 t1
JOIN ADW_Sales_orders t2 ON t1.CustomerID = t2.CustomerID
UNION
SELECT SalesOrderID, t1.CustomerID, TotalDue
FROM ADW_Top_10_spending_cust_2012 t1
JOIN ADW_Sales_orders t2 ON t1.CustomerID = t2.CustomerID

questions.title: Customers in the top 10 in both years
questions.story: How many customers are in the top 10 spenders of both 2011 and 2012?
approach: INNER JOIN the two top 10 tables on CustomerID. The rows that remain are the customers in both lists.
Count the rows (2 customers).

steps.sql:
SELECT t1.*
FROM ADW_Top_10_spending_cust_2011 t1
JOIN ADW_Top_10_spending_cust_2012 t2 ON t1.CustomerID = t2.CustomerID

questions.title: Orders bought for quality or supplier reputation
questions.story: The company wants to study buying behaviour. Find the orders placed for the reasons Quality or Manufacturer (supplier reputation) in 2012 and 2013.
approach: Look at ADW_Dim_Sales_Reason to find the two reasons: Quality and Manufacturer.
The path is ADW_Sales_orders, then ADW_Sales_orders_reasons, then ADW_Dim_Sales_Reason.
An order with both reasons appears twice, once per reason, so the result has more rows than orders. Drop ReasonName if you need one row per order.

steps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT t1.SalesOrderID, OrderDate, ReasonName
FROM ADW_Sales_orders t1
LEFT JOIN ADW_Sales_orders_reasons t2 ON t1.SalesOrderID = t2.SalesOrderID
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Sales_Reason t3 ON t2.SalesReasonID = t3.SalesReasonID
WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) IN (2012, 2013)
  AND ReasonName IN ('Quality', 'Manufacturer')

questions.title: Sold above 2,000 with a special offer
questions.story: The Business team wants to design a promotion for high-value purchases. Find the products that have been sold at a unit price above 2,000 and carried a special offer. Return ProductID and ProductName.
approach: The base table is ADW_Sales_orders_detail (sold products, UnitPrice, SpecialOfferID). Add ProductName from ADW_Dim_Product.
SpecialOfferID = 1 means 'No Discount', so a product with a special offer has SpecialOfferID <> 1. Check ADW_Dim_SpecialOffer to confirm.
You do not need to join ADW_Dim_SpecialOffer, because the ID is already in the detail table.

steps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT t1.ProductID, ProductName
FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail t1
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Product t3 ON t1.ProductID = t3.ProductID
WHERE SpecialOfferID != 1 AND UnitPrice > 2000

questions.title: Bikes and Clothing sold under a Volume Discount
questions.story: The Bikes and Clothing categories are planned for a cross-sell campaign. Find the names of the products in these two categories that sold under a Volume Discount offer.
approach: Same approach as the last question. The category IDs are 1 = Bikes and 3 = Clothing. The offer type is in the Type column of ADW_Dim_SpecialOffer.
Hard-coded IDs are quick but fragile. Look them up in ADW_Dim_ProductCategory first and say so in a comment.

steps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT t11.ProductName
FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail t1
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Product t11 ON t1.ProductID = t11.ProductID
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory t2
    ON CAST(t11.ProductSubcategoryID AS VARCHAR) = CAST(t2.ProductSubcategoryID AS VARCHAR)
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_SpecialOffer t5 ON t1.SpecialOfferID = t5.SpecialOfferID
WHERE t2.ProductCategoryID IN (1, 3)
  AND t5.[Type] = 'Volume Discount'

questions.title: Monthly revenue and profit report
questions.story: The board wants an overview of revenue, profit, profit margin and number of customers by month and year, across the four years the company has operated. Build the report.
approach: Metrics: revenue, profit, profit margin and customers. Dimensions: year and month.
Revenue = LineTotal (after discounts). Profit = revenue minus product cost (OrderQty x StandardCost). Margin = profit / revenue.
Customers per month cannot be added into a yearly total, because one customer buys in several months. Count the yearly figure with its own query.
Metric definitions can differ, so compare your logic with the model answer.

steps.sql:
SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS OrderYear,
       MONTH(OrderDate) AS OrderMonth,
       SUM(LineTotal) AS Revenue,
       SUM(t1.OrderQty*t3.StandardCost) AS Product_Cost,
       SUM(LineTotal - t1.OrderQty*t3.StandardCost) AS Profit,
       SUM(LineTotal - t1.OrderQty*t3.StandardCost)/SUM(LineTotal) AS Profit_margin,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) AS num_customers
FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail t1
LEFT JOIN ADW_Sales_orders t2 ON t1.SalesOrderID = t2.SalesOrderID
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Product t3 ON t1.ProductID = t3.ProductID
GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate)
ORDER BY OrderYear, OrderMonth

questions.title: Performance by country
questions.story: Build the same report by country and year: revenue, profit, customers and profit margin. Which country performs best and most steadily?
approach: Tables: sales order detail, sales order, product and territory.
Metrics: revenue, profit, customers and profit margin. Dimensions: year and country.
The query only produces the table. The answer to 'best and steadiest' is your reading of it. In this data Australia leads on margin every year, and the US has the most revenue but a thin margin.
2014 covers six months, so it is not comparable with full years.

steps.sql:
SELECT YEAR(t2.OrderDate) AS OrderYear,
       t4.CountryRegionCode,
       SUM(LineTotal) AS Revenue,
       SUM(LineTotal - t1.OrderQty*t3.StandardCost) AS Profit,
       SUM(LineTotal - t1.OrderQty*t3.StandardCost)/SUM(LineTotal) AS Profit_margin,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) AS num_customers
FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail t1
LEFT JOIN ADW_Sales_orders t2 ON t1.SalesOrderID = t2.SalesOrderID
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Product t3 ON t1.ProductID = t3.ProductID
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory t4 ON t2.TerritoryID = t4.TerritoryID
GROUP BY YEAR(t2.OrderDate), t4.CountryRegionCode
ORDER BY CountryRegionCode, OrderYear

questions.title: Revenue by payment method
questions.story: How much revenue does each payment method bring in, in each country?
approach: Metric: revenue. Dimensions: payment method and country.
Orders without a card (CreditCardID is the text 'NULL') count as cash payments.
In T-SQL the GROUP BY repeats the full CASE expression, because SELECT aliases are not available in GROUP BY.

steps.sql:
SELECT t2.CountryRegionCode AS Country,
       CASE WHEN t1.CreditCardID = 'NULL' OR t1.CreditCardID = '' THEN 'Cash' ELSE CardType END AS PaymentMethod,
       SUM(TotalDue) AS Revenue
FROM ADW_Sales_orders t1
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory t2 ON t1.TerritoryID = t2.TerritoryID
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_CreditCard t3 ON CAST(t1.CreditCardID AS VARCHAR) = CAST(t3.CreditCardID AS VARCHAR)
GROUP BY t2.CountryRegionCode,
         CASE WHEN t1.CreditCardID = 'NULL' OR t1.CreditCardID = '' THEN 'Cash' ELSE CardType END
ORDER BY Country, Revenue DESC

questions.title: Online share of revenue, 2013 vs 2014
questions.story: Compare the share of revenue that comes from the online channel in each country in 2013 and 2014. Where does online do best?
questions.hint: Use conditional aggregation to calculate online revenue as a share of total revenue.
approach: Metrics: online revenue, total revenue and online share. Dimensions: country and year.
Conditional aggregation: SUM(CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN ... END).
Use the same revenue column (TotalDue) for the numerator and the denominator.
2014 covers six months, so call it 'H1 2014' in the report.

steps.sql:
SELECT YEAR(t1.OrderDate) AS year,
       t2.CountryRegionCode AS Country,
       SUM(CASE WHEN t1.OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN TotalDue ELSE 0 END) AS Online_Revenue,
       SUM(TotalDue) AS Total_Revenue,
       SUM(CASE WHEN t1.OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN TotalDue ELSE 0 END)*100.00/SUM(TotalDue) AS Online_Revenue_Pct
FROM ADW_Sales_orders t1
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory t2 ON t1.TerritoryID = t2.TerritoryID
WHERE YEAR(t1.OrderDate) IN (2013, 2014)
GROUP BY t2.CountryRegionCode, YEAR(t1.OrderDate)
ORDER BY year, Online_Revenue_Pct DESC

questions.title: Weekdays vs weekends in the US
questions.story: The company wants to compare sales on weekdays and weekends in the US. For each US territory, compare the average quantity sold (OrderQty) per day and per customer on weekdays versus weekends. What do you notice in the numbers?
questions.hint: Use DATEPART together with CASE WHEN to label each day as a weekday or a weekend.
approach: In SQL Server, DATEPART(weekday, ...) returns 1 for Sunday and 7 for Saturday, so the weekend is (1, 7). Confirm it with SELECT DATEPART(weekday, '2026-09-15').
Numerator: OrderQty. Denominators: the number of days and the number of customers. Dimensions: territory and day type.
Divide by the number of days that actually had orders, not by 5 or 2.
Compare like with like. Some territories sell on only a few days, so their per-day figures describe a different business.

steps.sql:
SELECT TerritoryName,
       CASE WHEN DATEPART(weekday, OrderDate) IN (1,7) THEN 'Weekends' ELSE 'Weekdays' END AS DOW_type,
       SUM(t0.OrderQty*1.00)/COUNT(DISTINCT CAST(OrderDate AS DATE)) AS avg_daily_quantity,
       SUM(t0.OrderQty*1.00)/COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) AS avg_quantity_per_cust,
       COUNT(DISTINCT OrderDate) AS num_days
FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail t0
LEFT JOIN ADW_Sales_orders t1 ON t0.SalesOrderID = t1.SalesOrderID
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory t2 ON t1.TerritoryID = t2.TerritoryID
WHERE CountryRegionCode = 'US'
GROUP BY t2.TerritoryName,
         CASE WHEN DATEPART(weekday, OrderDate) IN (1,7) THEN 'Weekends' ELSE 'Weekdays' END
ORDER BY TerritoryName, DOW_type

questions.title: Buying behaviour, US vs EU
questions.story: The Customer Research team wants to compare buying behaviour in the US and the EU. Compare purchase frequency (orders per customer) and average quantity per order. Which region does better?
approach: Metrics: order frequency (orders per customer) and average quantity per order. Dimension: region (EU or US).
Multiply by 1.00 to avoid integer division.
Use DISTINCT when you count orders, or each order is counted once per product line.
'Better' is not one number. Say which metric you rank by.

steps.sql:
SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS OrderYear,
       CASE WHEN [Group] = 'Europe' THEN 'EU' ELSE 'US' END AS Region,
       COUNT(DISTINCT t1.SalesOrderID)*1.00/COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) AS OrderFrequency,
       SUM(t1.OrderQty)*1.00/COUNT(DISTINCT t1.SalesOrderID) AS AvgQtyPerOrder
FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail t1
LEFT JOIN ADW_Sales_orders t2 ON t1.SalesOrderID = t2.SalesOrderID
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory t3 ON t2.TerritoryID = t3.TerritoryID
WHERE [Group] = 'Europe' OR CountryRegionCode = 'US'
GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate), CASE WHEN [Group] = 'Europe' THEN 'EU' ELSE 'US' END
ORDER BY OrderYear, Region

questions.title: Which category to push in Europe
questions.story: If the company wants to push one category in Europe, which one should it be?
questions.hint: This is an open question. Look at it from more than one angle, for example revenue, profit and profit margin.
approach: When the question does not name the metric, use business sense: revenue, profit, profit margin and orders.
Dimension: product category, filtered to Europe.

Back your recommendation with two views. Bikes carry almost all of the profit. Accessories have the best margin and the most orders, but a small order value. 'Bikes for profit, Accessories as the high-margin add-on' is a reasonable answer.
Add the year to the GROUP BY to see whether the picture is stable.

steps.sql:
SELECT ProductCategoryName,
       SUM(LineTotal) AS Revenue,
       SUM(LineTotal) - SUM(t3.StandardCost*t1.OrderQty) AS Profit,
       (SUM(LineTotal) - SUM(t3.StandardCost*t1.OrderQty))/SUM(LineTotal) AS Profit_margin,
       COUNT(DISTINCT t1.SalesOrderID) AS Orders,
       SUM(LineTotal)/COUNT(DISTINCT t1.SalesOrderID) AS AOV
FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail t1
LEFT JOIN ADW_Sales_orders t2 ON t1.SalesOrderID = t2.SalesOrderID
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Product t3 ON t1.ProductID = t3.ProductID
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory t4 ON t3.ProductSubcategoryID = CAST(t4.ProductSubcategoryID AS VARCHAR)
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductCategory t5 ON CAST(t4.ProductCategoryID AS VARCHAR) = CAST(t5.ProductCategoryID AS VARCHAR)
LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory t6 ON t2.TerritoryID = t6.TerritoryID
WHERE [Group] = 'Europe'
GROUP BY ProductCategoryName

questions.title: Customers with AOV above the US AOV
questions.story: The company wants to target customers whose average order value (AOV) is higher than the AOV of customers who buy in the US, to study how to raise AOV. List these customers.
questions.hint: AOV = total value of all orders divided by the number of orders.
approach: Step 1: calculate the AOV of US customers. It is one number (a scalar).
Step 2: use it as the condition in the main query, through a subquery or a CTE.
Order value can be SubTotal or TotalDue, and the choice moves the threshold. Pick one and state it.
Multiply by 1.00 so the division is not an integer division.

steps.title: CTE
steps.sql:
WITH AOV_in_US AS (
    SELECT SUM(SubTotal)*1.00/COUNT(SalesOrderID) AS AOV_US
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders t1
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory t2 ON t1.TerritoryID = t2.TerritoryID
    WHERE CountryRegionCode = 'US'
),
AOV_all AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, SUM(SubTotal)*1.00/COUNT(SalesOrderID) AS AOV
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID
)
SELECT *
FROM AOV_all
WHERE AOV > (SELECT * FROM AOV_in_US)
ORDER BY AOV DESC

steps.title: Subquery
steps.sql:
SELECT CustomerID, SUM(SubTotal)*1.00/COUNT(SalesOrderID) AS AOV
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
GROUP BY CustomerID
HAVING SUM(SubTotal)*1.00/COUNT(SalesOrderID) >
(
    SELECT SUM(SubTotal)*1.00/COUNT(SalesOrderID)
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders t1
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory t2 ON t1.TerritoryID = t2.TerritoryID
    WHERE CountryRegionCode = 'US'
)
ORDER BY AOV DESC

questions.title: Bikes only, Clothing only, or both
questions.story:
Split customers into three groups and compare the average order value (AOV) of their Bikes and Clothing purchases.
- Group 1: bought only Bikes.
- Group 2: bought both Bikes and Clothing.
- Group 3: bought only Clothing.
approach: Step 1: use conditional aggregation to count each customer's Bikes orders and Clothing orders.
Step 2: use CASE WHEN to put each customer in one of the three groups.
Step 3: calculate the AOV for each group. Split the steps into CTEs you can reuse.
Spending and orders count only Bikes and Clothing lines, not the whole basket. Count DISTINCT SalesOrderID, so an order is not counted once per product line.

steps.sql:
WITH order_stats AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           SUM(LineTotal) AS TotalSpending,
           COUNT(DISTINCT t1.SalesOrderID) AS Total_orders,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN ProductCategoryName = 'Bikes' THEN t1.SalesOrderID END) AS Bikes_orders,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN ProductCategoryName = 'Clothing' THEN t1.SalesOrderID END) AS Clothing_orders
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail t1
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Sales_orders t2 ON t1.SalesOrderID = t2.SalesOrderID
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Product t3 ON t1.ProductID = t3.ProductID
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory t4 ON t3.ProductSubcategoryID = CAST(t4.ProductSubcategoryID AS NVARCHAR)
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductCategory t5 ON t4.ProductCategoryID = t5.ProductCategoryID
    WHERE ProductCategoryName IN ('Bikes', 'Clothing')
    GROUP BY CustomerID
),
customer_group_tab AS (
    SELECT *,
           CASE WHEN Bikes_orders > 0 AND Clothing_orders = 0 THEN '1. Bikes Only'
                WHEN Bikes_orders = 0 AND Clothing_orders > 0 THEN '2. Clothing Only'
                WHEN Bikes_orders > 0 AND Clothing_orders > 0 THEN '3. Bikes & Clothing'
           END AS customer_groups
    FROM order_stats
)
SELECT customer_groups, CustomerID, SUM(TotalSpending)/SUM(Total_orders) AS AOV
FROM customer_group_tab
GROUP BY CustomerID, customer_groups

questions.title: Year-over-year growth by country
questions.story: Calculate year-over-year revenue growth (% YoY) by country for 2012 to 2014. Which country grows fastest?
approach: Expected columns: year, country, current-year revenue, last-year revenue and YoY growth.
Method 1 (less efficient): CTE and self join with an unequal join (OrderYear = OrderYear + 1). Method 2: the window function LAG.
The two methods use different revenue definitions (SubTotal and LineTotal), so the numbers differ slightly.
2014 is a half year, so its growth compares six months with twelve. Compare 2012 and 2013, or the same months.
Small bases inflate percentages, so show the absolute revenue too.

steps.title: Method 1: CTE + self join
steps.sql:
WITH country_revenue_by_year AS (
    SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS OrderYear, CountryRegionCode, SUM(SubTotal) AS Revenue
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders t1
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory t5 ON t1.TerritoryID = t5.TerritoryID
    GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate), CountryRegionCode
)
SELECT t1.*,
       t2.Revenue AS previous_year_revenue,
       CASE WHEN t2.Revenue IS NOT NULL THEN t1.Revenue/t2.Revenue - 1 ELSE 0 END AS YOY_growth
FROM country_revenue_by_year t1
LEFT JOIN country_revenue_by_year t2
       ON t1.CountryRegionCode = t2.CountryRegionCode
      AND t1.OrderYear = t2.OrderYear + 1
WHERE t1.OrderYear BETWEEN 2012 AND 2014
ORDER BY CountryRegionCode DESC, OrderYear

steps.title: Method 2: window function LAG
steps.sql:
WITH Country_Revenue AS (
    SELECT T3.CountryRegionCode AS Country, YEAR(T1.OrderDate) AS OrderYear, SUM(T2.LineTotal) AS CurentRevenue
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders T1
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Sales_orders_detail T2 ON T1.SalesOrderID = T2.SalesOrderID
    INNER JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory T3 ON T1.TerritoryID = T3.TerritoryID
    WHERE YEAR(T1.OrderDate) BETWEEN 2011 AND 2014
    GROUP BY T3.CountryRegionCode, YEAR(T1.OrderDate)
),
Country_Revenue_Add AS (
    SELECT *, LAG(CurentRevenue) OVER (PARTITION BY Country ORDER BY OrderYear) AS PreviousRevenue
    FROM Country_Revenue
)
SELECT Country, OrderYear, CurentRevenue, (CurentRevenue/PreviousRevenue) - 1 AS YOYGrowthPercentage
FROM Country_Revenue_Add
WHERE OrderYear BETWEEN 2012 AND 2014
ORDER BY Country, OrderYear

questions.title: Sub-categories with rising promotion cost
questions.story: The company is reviewing the total promotion cost of its sub-categories. List the sub-categories whose total promotion cost rose two years in a row.
questions.hint: It works like the year-over-year question (HW 3).
approach: Metrics: promotion cost in the current year, the next year and the year after. Dimensions: year and sub-category.
Promotion cost = UnitPriceDiscount x UnitPrice x OrderQty.
Method 1: CTE and self join. Method 2: LEAD().
Gap risk: HAVING removes years with zero promotion, so the next row may not be the next year. Check that the years are consecutive.

steps.title: Method 2: LEAD
steps.sql:
WITH promotion_cost_by_year_sub_cate AS (
    SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS OrderYear,
           ProductSubCategoryName,
           SUM(UnitPriceDiscount*UnitPrice*OrderQty) AS Total_promo_cost_current_year
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail t1
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Sales_orders t2 ON t1.SalesOrderID = t2.SalesOrderID
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Product t3 ON t1.ProductID = t3.ProductID
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory t4
        ON CAST(T3.ProductSubcategoryID AS VARCHAR) = CAST(T4.ProductSubcategoryID AS VARCHAR)
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductCategory t5 ON t4.ProductCategoryID = t5.ProductCategoryID
    GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate), ProductSubCategoryName
    HAVING SUM(UnitPriceDiscount*UnitPrice*OrderQty) > 0
),
YearGrowth AS (
    SELECT *,
           LEAD(Total_promo_cost_current_year, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY ProductSubCategoryName ORDER BY OrderYear) AS Promo_cost_next_1_year,
           LEAD(Total_promo_cost_current_year, 2) OVER (PARTITION BY ProductSubCategoryName ORDER BY OrderYear) AS Promo_cost_next_2_year
    FROM promotion_cost_by_year_sub_cate
)
SELECT *
FROM YearGrowth
WHERE Total_promo_cost_current_year > 0
  AND Promo_cost_next_1_year > Total_promo_cost_current_year
  AND Promo_cost_next_2_year > Promo_cost_next_1_year

questions.title: Running revenue by category
questions.story: Review the accumulated (running) revenue of each category, month by month within each year. Build the report.
questions.hint: Use an aggregate window function.
approach: Expected columns: year, month, category, revenue and accumulated revenue.
Window: PARTITION BY category and year, ORDER BY month. Function: SUM.
With ORDER BY, the default frame runs from the first row to the current row. That is what makes it a running total.
Months with no sales do not appear, and the running total simply skips them.

steps.sql:
WITH monthly_rev_by_cate AS (
    SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS OrderYear,
           MONTH(OrderDate) AS OrderMonth,
           ProductCategoryName AS Category,
           SUM(LineTotal) AS Revenue
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail t1
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Sales_orders t2 ON t1.SalesOrderID = t2.SalesOrderID
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Product t3 ON t1.ProductID = t3.ProductID
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory t4 ON CAST(t3.ProductSubcategoryID AS VARCHAR) = CAST(t4.ProductSubcategoryID AS VARCHAR)
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductCategory AS t5 ON t4.ProductCategoryID = t5.ProductCategoryID
    GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), ProductCategoryName
)
SELECT OrderYear, OrderMonth, Category,
       Revenue AS MonthlyRevenue,
       SUM(Revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY OrderYear, Category ORDER BY OrderMonth) AS AccumulatedRevenue
FROM monthly_rev_by_cate

questions.title: Best-selling product by country
questions.story: Which product sold the most units in each country?
approach: Step 1: a base CTE with product name, country and units sold.
Step 2: RANK() or DENSE_RANK() with PARTITION BY country and ORDER BY units sold descending, then keep rank 1.
Use RANK or DENSE_RANK so that ties all appear. ROW_NUMBER would hide a tie for first place.
Put the rank filter outside the window query, because WHERE runs before window functions.

steps.sql:
WITH product_sold_by_product_country AS (
    SELECT ProductName, CountryRegionCode AS Country, SUM(OrderQty) AS Product_sold
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail T1
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Sales_orders T2 ON T1.SalesOrderID = T2.SalesOrderID
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Product T3 ON T1.ProductID = T3.ProductID
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory t4 ON t2.TerritoryID = t4.TerritoryID
    GROUP BY ProductName, CountryRegionCode
)
SELECT ProductName, Country, Product_sold
FROM (
    SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY Country ORDER BY Product_sold DESC) AS Product_sold_ranking
    FROM product_sold_by_product_country
) t
WHERE t.Product_sold_ranking = 1

questions.title: Month-over-month growth by category
questions.story: Calculate month-over-month (MoM) revenue growth for each category across the years. January must be compared with the previous December.
approach: Window: PARTITION BY category, ORDER BY year and month, so January looks back to December. Function: LAG.
MoM = revenue / previous month revenue - 1.
Partitioning by year as well would leave every January without a previous month.
LAG compares neighbouring rows, not neighbouring calendar months, so a month with no sales is skipped. Use NULL, not 0, when there is no previous month.

steps.sql:
WITH Revenue_by_cate_month AS (
    SELECT ProductCategoryName, YEAR(OrderDate) AS OrderYear, MONTH(OrderDate) AS OrderMonth, SUM(LineTotal) AS Revenue
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail t1
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Sales_orders t2 ON t1.SalesOrderID = t2.SalesOrderID
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Product t3 ON t1.ProductID = t3.ProductID
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory t4 ON TRY_CAST(t3.ProductSubcategoryID AS INT) = t4.ProductSubcategoryID
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductCategory t5 ON t4.ProductCategoryID = t5.ProductCategoryID
    GROUP BY ProductCategoryName, MONTH(OrderDate), YEAR(OrderDate)
),
Revenue_Prev_month AS (
    SELECT *, LAG(Revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY ProductCategoryName ORDER BY OrderYear, OrderMonth) AS prev_month_revenue
    FROM Revenue_by_cate_month
)
SELECT *,
       CASE WHEN prev_month_revenue IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE Revenue/prev_month_revenue - 1 END AS MoM_growth
FROM Revenue_Prev_month

questions.title: Spending above the Clothing median
questions.story: Find the customers whose total spending across all categories is above the 50th percentile of spending among Clothing customers.
questions.hint:
Step 1: find the 50th percentile of spending among Clothing customers (expected output: one number) with PERCENT_RANK().
Step 2: calculate each customer's total spending in all categories and keep the customers above the number from step 1.
approach: Base CTE: customer, category and spending.
PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY spending) on the Clothing rows only. The 50th percentile is the smallest spending with a percent rank of 0.5 or more.
The median Clothing spend is small, so most customers pass. Say so when you report the number.
The window runs on Clothing only because the WHERE sits inside that CTE. Move it out and the percentile covers every category.

steps.sql:
WITH Customers_spending AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, ProductCategoryName, SUM(LineTotal) AS Spending
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail t1
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Sales_orders t2 ON t1.SalesOrderID = t2.SalesOrderID
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Product t3 ON t1.ProductID = t3.ProductID
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory t4 ON CAST(t3.ProductSubcategoryID AS VARCHAR) = CAST(t4.ProductSubcategoryID AS VARCHAR)
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductCategory t5 ON t4.ProductCategoryID = t5.ProductCategoryID
    GROUP BY CustomerID, ProductCategoryName
),
clothing_spending_pct_rank AS (
    SELECT *, PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Spending) AS spending_pct
    FROM Customers_spending
    WHERE ProductCategoryName = 'Clothing'
),
spending_condition AS (
    SELECT MIN(Spending) AS P50_clothing_spending
    FROM clothing_spending_pct_rank
    WHERE spending_pct >= 0.5
)
SELECT CustomerID, SUM(Spending) AS total_spending_all_cate
FROM Customers_spending
GROUP BY CustomerID
HAVING SUM(Spending) > (SELECT * FROM spending_condition)
ORDER BY total_spending_all_cate

questions.title: Most popular payment method
questions.story: Which payment method is the most popular by number of orders in each country and year? If you rank by total revenue instead, does the order change?
approach: Base CTE: year, country, payment method, orders and revenue.
Window: PARTITION BY country and year. DENSE_RANK() by orders and by revenue, then compare the two ranks.
Two windows in one SELECT can have different ORDER BY clauses.
Ties appear when two methods have the same order count. DENSE_RANK keeps both at rank 1.

steps.sql:
WITH payment_base AS (
    SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS OrderYear,
           CountryRegionCode AS Country,
           CASE WHEN CardType IS NULL THEN 'Cash' ELSE CardType END AS PaymentMethod,
           COUNT(DISTINCT SalesOrderID) AS Orders,
           SUM(SubTotal) AS Revenue
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders t1
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory t2 ON t1.TerritoryID = t2.TerritoryID
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_CreditCard t3 ON t1.CreditCardID = CAST(t3.CreditCardID AS VARCHAR)
    GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate), CountryRegionCode, CASE WHEN CardType IS NULL THEN 'Cash' ELSE CardType END
),
ranking_base AS (
    SELECT *,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY Country, OrderYear ORDER BY Orders DESC) AS RankByOrders,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY Country, OrderYear ORDER BY Revenue DESC) AS RankByRevenue
    FROM payment_base
)
SELECT *,
       CASE WHEN RankByOrders = 1 AND RankByRevenue = 1 THEN '1. Top By BOTH'
            WHEN RankByOrders = 1 AND RankByRevenue > 1 THEN '2. Top By Orders'
            ELSE '3. Top By Revenue' END AS group_ranking
FROM ranking_base
WHERE RankByOrders = 1 OR RankByRevenue = 1

questions.title: Top 5 promoted products by territory
questions.story: Review the promotion programme of each territory. For each territory, list the 5 products with the highest share of units sold with a promotion.
approach: Base CTE: territory, product, units sold, units sold with a promotion, and the share sold with a promotion.
Window: PARTITION BY territory, ORDER BY share descending, DENSE_RANK(), then keep rank 5 or lower.
The model answer combines all years. To see each year, add YEAR(OrderDate) to the GROUP BY and to the PARTITION BY.
A product sold once with a discount has a 100% share. Consider a minimum quantity before ranking.

steps.sql:
WITH quantity_by_product_territory AS (
    SELECT TerritoryName,
           ProductName,
           SUM(OrderQty) AS product_sold,
           SUM(CASE WHEN t1.UnitPriceDiscount > 0 THEN OrderQty ELSE 0 END) AS product_sold_with_promotion,
           SUM(CASE WHEN t1.UnitPriceDiscount > 0 THEN OrderQty ELSE 0 END)*1.00/SUM(OrderQty) AS product_sold_with_promotion_pct
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail t1
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Sales_orders t2 ON t1.SalesOrderID = t2.SalesOrderID
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Product t3 ON t1.ProductID = t3.ProductID
    LEFT JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory t6 ON t2.TerritoryID = t6.TerritoryID
    GROUP BY TerritoryName, ProductName
)
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT *, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY TerritoryName ORDER BY product_sold_with_promotion_pct DESC) AS pct_promo_rank
    FROM quantity_by_product_territory
) t
WHERE pct_promo_rank <= 5

questions.title: Orders with no salesperson
questions.story: Finance wants to know how many orders were placed without a salesperson, to see how much revenue comes from direct sales. Return the number of orders with no salesperson and the total number of orders.
questions.hint: Run SELECT DISTINCT SalesPersonID FROM ADW_Sales_orders first and read the values. In this database a missing salesperson is stored as the text 'NULL', so IS NULL finds nothing.
approach: The column is SalesPersonID in ADW_Sales_orders.
A missing value here is the text 'NULL', not a real NULL. Compare with = 'NULL'.
Get both numbers in one query: SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) for the missing ones and COUNT(*) for the total.
All 27,659 online orders have no salesperson, and every reseller order has one.

steps.sql:
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN SalesPersonID = 'NULL' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS orders_without_salesperson,
       COUNT(*) AS total_orders
FROM ADW_Sales_orders

questions.title: Products with no colour
questions.story: The product team wants to see how many products there are in each colour. Products with a missing colour should show as 'Unknown'. Return the colour and the number of products.
questions.hint: As in the last question, a missing colour is the text 'NULL'. Replace it with CASE WHEN, then group by the new column.
approach: The column is Color in ADW_Dim_Product.
CASE WHEN Color = 'NULL' THEN 'Unknown' ELSE Color END gives a clean colour.
T-SQL does not allow a SELECT alias in GROUP BY. Build the clean column in a CTE or subquery first, then group by it.
There are 10 rows. 248 products have no colour.

steps.sql:
WITH products AS (
    SELECT CASE WHEN Color = 'NULL' THEN 'Unknown' ELSE Color END AS color_clean
    FROM ADW_Dim_Product
)
SELECT color_clean, COUNT(*) AS products
FROM products
GROUP BY color_clean

questions.title: Fix the typos in the account list
questions.story: Sales Ops found spelling mistakes in the account list. Return every account with a clean sector and a clean office location. Change 'technolgy' to 'technology' and 'Philipines' to 'Philippines', and keep every other value as it is.
questions.hint: Run SELECT DISTINCT sector FROM CRM_Accounts and SELECT DISTINCT office_location FROM CRM_Accounts first, and read each list slowly.
approach: Both columns are in CRM_Accounts.
Use CASE WHEN to remap only the wrong value and leave the rest unchanged. REPLACE also works.
Return all 85 accounts. 12 have the sector typo and 1 has the location typo.
Do not drop rows because of a typo. Fix the value instead.

steps.sql:
SELECT account,
       CASE WHEN sector = 'technolgy' THEN 'technology' ELSE sector END AS sector_clean,
       CASE WHEN office_location = 'Philipines' THEN 'Philippines' ELSE office_location END AS office_location_clean
FROM CRM_Accounts

questions.title: Deals lost in a join
questions.story: In Lesson 3 you listed the 2017 won deals priced above the list price and got 1,674. That count missed deals, because the pipeline writes one product as 'GTXPro' and the product list writes 'GTX Pro'. Fix the name and join again. For won deals closed in 2017, return three numbers: how many deals there are, how many found a list price, and how many closed above the list price.
questions.hint: Use REPLACE(product, 'GTXPro', 'GTX Pro') in the join condition. After the fix, the number of deals that found a price should equal the number of won deals.
approach: Deals are in CRM_sales_pipeline and list prices are in CRM_products.
A LEFT JOIN keeps every deal, so unmatched deals show up as a NULL price. That is how you find the problem.
Count the matches before and after the fix. A join that silently drops rows is a data quality issue, not a result.
After the fix, all 4,238 deals find a price and 2,040 closed above it.

steps.title: Fix the name and join
steps.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS won_deals_2017,
       SUM(CASE WHEN t2.product IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS deals_with_price,
       SUM(CASE WHEN t1.close_value > t2.sales_price THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS above_list_price
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline t1
LEFT JOIN CRM_products t2
    ON REPLACE(t1.product, 'GTXPro', 'GTX Pro') = t2.product
WHERE t1.deal_stage = 'Won'
  AND YEAR(t1.close_date) = 2017

questions.note: 4,238 deals, 4,238 with a price, 2,040 above list price

questions.title: Customers by age group
questions.story: Marketing plans an age-based campaign. In GBE_Customers the birthday is stored as text, for example 7/3/1939. Convert it to a date and work out each customer's age on 2020-01-01. Then count customers in four groups: Under 30, 30-49, 50-69 and 70+. Return the group name and the number of customers.
questions.hint: CONVERT(date, Birthday, 101) turns text like 7/3/1939 into a date. CAST(Birthday AS DATE) does not work on this format here.
approach: The column is Birthday in GBE_Customers. It is text in month/day/year order.
Age = DATEDIFF(year, birth date, '2020-01-01').
Groups: Under 30 means age below 30, 30-49 means 30 to 49, 50-69 means 50 to 69, 70+ means 70 and over. Use these labels exactly.
Calculate the age in a CTE, label the groups in a second step, then count.
The four groups add up to 15,266 customers.

steps.sql:
WITH ages AS (
    SELECT DATEDIFF(year, CONVERT(date, Birthday, 101), '2020-01-01') AS age
    FROM GBE_Customers
),
grouped AS (
    SELECT CASE WHEN age < 30 THEN 'Under 30'
                WHEN age < 50 THEN '30-49'
                WHEN age < 70 THEN '50-69'
                ELSE '70+' END AS age_group
    FROM ages
)
SELECT age_group, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM grouped
GROUP BY age_group

questions.title: Repeated customer names
questions.story: The data team thinks GBE_Customers contains duplicate customers, because 15,266 customers have only 15,118 different names. Check it. For each name that appears more than once, return the name, how many times it is listed, and how many different birthdays it has.
questions.hint: GROUP BY Name with HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. COUNT(DISTINCT Birthday) counts the different birthdays.
approach: The table is GBE_Customers. Each customer already has a unique CustomerKey.
A repeated name is not enough to call two rows duplicates. Compare another field, here the birthday.
137 names appear more than once, and every repeat has a different birthday. These are different people, so nothing should be deleted.
Count before you delete.

steps.sql:
SELECT Name,
       COUNT(*) AS times_listed,
       COUNT(DISTINCT Birthday) AS different_birthdays
FROM GBE_Customers
GROUP BY Name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1

questions.note: 137 names, each repeat has a different birthday

questions.title: Orders far above average
questions.story: Finance wants to review unusually large orders before the monthly report. Flag an order as an outlier when its TotalDue is more than 2 standard deviations above the average TotalDue of all orders. Return how many orders are flagged and how many orders there are in total.
questions.hint: STDEV(TotalDue) gives the standard deviation. Calculate the average and STDEV in a CTE or subquery, then compare each order with average + 2 x STDEV.
approach: The column is TotalDue in ADW_Sales_orders.
Upper limit = AVG(TotalDue) + 2 * STDEV(TotalDue). Use STDEV, the sample standard deviation.
Compare every order with that one number. A CTE with the limit, cross joined to the orders, keeps the query readable.
1,323 of 31,465 orders (4.2%) are flagged.

steps.sql:
WITH limits AS (
    SELECT AVG(TotalDue) + 2 * STDEV(TotalDue) AS upper_limit
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
)
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN o.TotalDue > l.upper_limit THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS outlier_orders,
       COUNT(*) AS total_orders
FROM ADW_Sales_orders o
CROSS JOIN limits l

questions.title: Two ways to find outliers
questions.story: Repeat the outlier check with the IQR rule. An order is an outlier when TotalDue is above Q3 + 1.5 x IQR, where IQR = Q3 - Q1. Compare the number of flagged orders with the standard deviation method from the last question. Which method flags more orders, and why? Would you remove these orders? Write your conclusion below.
questions.hint: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.25) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY TotalDue) OVER () gives Q1. Use 0.75 for Q3.
approach: Q1 and Q3 are the 25th and 75th percentiles of TotalDue. Calculate them in a CTE.
The lower limit (Q1 - 1.5 x IQR) is below zero, so no order can be flagged on the low side.
IQR flags 2,127 orders and the standard deviation method flags 1,323. TotalDue is skewed, and a few very large orders inflate the standard deviation, so the SD limit sits higher.
Every flagged order is a reseller order, so these are real large sales and not errors. Investigate before you remove anything.

steps.title: Compare the two methods
steps.sql:
WITH sd_limit AS (
    SELECT AVG(TotalDue) + 2 * STDEV(TotalDue) AS upper_limit
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
),
quartiles AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT
           PERCENTILE_CONT(0.25) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY TotalDue) OVER () AS q1,
           PERCENTILE_CONT(0.75) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY TotalDue) OVER () AS q3
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
)
SELECT 'Standard deviation' AS method, COUNT(*) AS flagged_orders
FROM ADW_Sales_orders o
CROSS JOIN sd_limit l
WHERE o.TotalDue > l.upper_limit
UNION ALL
SELECT 'IQR', COUNT(*)
FROM ADW_Sales_orders o
CROSS JOIN quartiles q
WHERE o.TotalDue > q.q3 + 1.5 * (q.q3 - q.q1)

questions.title: Validate the cleaned accounts
questions.story: Before you share the cleaned account list from the typo question, validate it. Return one row with four numbers: the total number of rows, the number of different accounts, the rows where the sector is still 'technolgy', and the rows where the office location is still 'Philipines'.
questions.hint: Rebuild the cleaned list in a CTE, then count on top of it. The validation must run on the cleaned data, not on CRM_Accounts.
approach: Validation answers one question: did the cleaning do what you meant, and did it break anything else?
Check the row count (still 85), duplicates (85 different accounts) and the bad values that should be gone (0 and 0).
If you run the same checks on the raw table, you get 12 sector typos and 1 location typo. That is the before and after.

steps.sql:
WITH accounts_clean AS (
    SELECT account,
           CASE WHEN sector = 'technolgy' THEN 'technology' ELSE sector END AS sector_clean,
           CASE WHEN office_location = 'Philipines' THEN 'Philippines' ELSE office_location END AS location_clean
    FROM CRM_Accounts
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows,
       COUNT(DISTINCT account) AS distinct_accounts,
       SUM(CASE WHEN sector_clean = 'technolgy' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS sector_typos_left,
       SUM(CASE WHEN location_clean = 'Philipines' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS location_typos_left
FROM accounts_clean

questions.title: R, F and M for every customer
questions.story: Marketing wants to segment customers by how recently, how often and how much they buy. Start with the raw numbers. For every customer in ADW_Sales_orders, return Recency (days between the customer's last order and 2014-07-01), Frequency (number of orders) and Monetary (total TotalDue).
questions.hint: DATEDIFF(day, MAX(OrderDate), '2014-07-01'), COUNT(DISTINCT SalesOrderID) and SUM(TotalDue), all grouped by CustomerID.
approach: Everything is in ADW_Sales_orders. Group by CustomerID.
2014-07-01 is the snapshot date, the day after the last order in the data. Recency is smaller for customers who bought recently.
Frequency counts orders, not product lines. Monetary adds up TotalDue.
There are 19,119 customers. 11,649 of them (61%) bought only once.

steps.sql:
SELECT CustomerID,
       DATEDIFF(day, MAX(OrderDate), '2014-07-01') AS Recency,
       COUNT(DISTINCT SalesOrderID) AS Frequency,
       SUM(TotalDue) AS Monetary
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
GROUP BY CustomerID

questions.title: Score each customer from 1 to 5
questions.story: Turn the three numbers into scores. For each customer, calculate PERCENT_RANK for Recency, Frequency and Monetary, then cut each percentile into five bands: up to 0.2 is 1, up to 0.4 is 2, up to 0.6 is 3, up to 0.8 is 4, and above 0.8 is 5. A recent customer must get a high Recency score, so rank Recency from the most days to the fewest (ORDER BY Recency DESC). Return CustomerID, R_score, F_score and M_score.
questions.hint: Put the R, F and M calculation from the last question in a CTE. Then use three PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY ...) columns and a CASE WHEN for each band.
approach: Step 1: R, F and M per customer (the last question) as a CTE.
Step 2: PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Recency DESC), (ORDER BY Frequency) and (ORDER BY Monetary), in a second CTE.
Step 3: a CASE WHEN for each percentile with the bands 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8.
Ties land in the same band, so the bands are not equal in size. 61% of customers bought once, so the Frequency score only takes the values 1, 4 and 5.

steps.sql:
WITH rfm AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           DATEDIFF(day, MAX(OrderDate), '2014-07-01') AS Recency,
           COUNT(DISTINCT SalesOrderID) AS Frequency,
           SUM(TotalDue) AS Monetary
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID
),
percentiles AS (
    SELECT *,
           PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Recency DESC) AS r_pct,
           PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Frequency) AS f_pct,
           PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Monetary) AS m_pct
    FROM rfm
),
scores AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           CASE WHEN r_pct <= 0.2 THEN 1 WHEN r_pct <= 0.4 THEN 2 WHEN r_pct <= 0.6 THEN 3 WHEN r_pct <= 0.8 THEN 4 ELSE 5 END AS R_score,
           CASE WHEN f_pct <= 0.2 THEN 1 WHEN f_pct <= 0.4 THEN 2 WHEN f_pct <= 0.6 THEN 3 WHEN f_pct <= 0.8 THEN 4 ELSE 5 END AS F_score,
           CASE WHEN m_pct <= 0.2 THEN 1 WHEN m_pct <= 0.4 THEN 2 WHEN m_pct <= 0.6 THEN 3 WHEN m_pct <= 0.8 THEN 4 ELSE 5 END AS M_score
    FROM percentiles
)
SELECT CustomerID, R_score, F_score, M_score
FROM scores

questions.title: Size and value of each segment
questions.story:
Marketing needs a simple segment list. Using the scores from the last question, put each customer in the first segment they match:
- Champions: R, F and M scores are all 4 or 5.
- Loyal: F score is 4 or 5.
- Promising: R score is 4 or 5.
- At Risk: M score is 4 or 5.
- Hibernating: everyone else.
For each segment, return the number of customers, the number of orders and the total revenue (TotalDue).
questions.hint: A CASE WHEN checks the conditions from top to bottom, and the first true one wins. Join the segments back to ADW_Sales_orders on CustomerID to count orders and add up revenue.
approach: Build the scores as in the last question, then add a segment with CASE WHEN in the order above.
Join back to ADW_Sales_orders on CustomerID. Customers are counted with COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID), orders with COUNT of SalesOrderID.
The 2,426 Champions are 13% of customers and bring about 69% of the revenue.
Hibernating is the biggest segment (6,266 customers) and the smallest in revenue.

steps.sql:
WITH rfm AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           DATEDIFF(day, MAX(OrderDate), '2014-07-01') AS Recency,
           COUNT(DISTINCT SalesOrderID) AS Frequency,
           SUM(TotalDue) AS Monetary
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID
),
percentiles AS (
    SELECT *,
           PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Recency DESC) AS r_pct,
           PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Frequency) AS f_pct,
           PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Monetary) AS m_pct
    FROM rfm
),
scores AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           CASE WHEN r_pct <= 0.2 THEN 1 WHEN r_pct <= 0.4 THEN 2 WHEN r_pct <= 0.6 THEN 3 WHEN r_pct <= 0.8 THEN 4 ELSE 5 END AS R_score,
           CASE WHEN f_pct <= 0.2 THEN 1 WHEN f_pct <= 0.4 THEN 2 WHEN f_pct <= 0.6 THEN 3 WHEN f_pct <= 0.8 THEN 4 ELSE 5 END AS F_score,
           CASE WHEN m_pct <= 0.2 THEN 1 WHEN m_pct <= 0.4 THEN 2 WHEN m_pct <= 0.6 THEN 3 WHEN m_pct <= 0.8 THEN 4 ELSE 5 END AS M_score
    FROM percentiles
),
segments AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           CASE WHEN R_score >= 4 AND F_score >= 4 AND M_score >= 4 THEN 'Champions'
                WHEN F_score >= 4 THEN 'Loyal'
                WHEN R_score >= 4 THEN 'Promising'
                WHEN M_score >= 4 THEN 'At Risk'
                ELSE 'Hibernating' END AS segment
    FROM scores
)
SELECT s.segment,
       COUNT(DISTINCT s.CustomerID) AS customers,
       COUNT(o.SalesOrderID) AS orders,
       SUM(o.TotalDue) AS revenue
FROM segments s
JOIN ADW_Sales_orders o ON s.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
GROUP BY s.segment

questions.title: How each segment buys
questions.story: The CRM team asks if there is any notable buying behaviour in each segment. For each segment from the last question, return the average order value (AOV), the number of orders per customer and the share of orders placed online. Then write two findings and one action for the team.
questions.hint: AOV = total TotalDue divided by the number of orders. The online share uses OnlineOrderFlag, which is 1 for online orders.
approach: Reuse the segment CTEs and join to ADW_Sales_orders.
Multiply by 1.0 so the divisions are not integer divisions.
Champions have the highest AOV (about 11,000) and the most orders per customer (3.2), and 39% of their orders are offline, so many of them are resellers.

Hibernating, Promising and At Risk customers have exactly one order each and are 99% online. At Risk customers spend about 2,650 per order, four times the Promising average. They are the first win-back target.

steps.sql:
WITH rfm AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           DATEDIFF(day, MAX(OrderDate), '2014-07-01') AS Recency,
           COUNT(DISTINCT SalesOrderID) AS Frequency,
           SUM(TotalDue) AS Monetary
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID
),
percentiles AS (
    SELECT *,
           PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Recency DESC) AS r_pct,
           PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Frequency) AS f_pct,
           PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Monetary) AS m_pct
    FROM rfm
),
scores AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           CASE WHEN r_pct <= 0.2 THEN 1 WHEN r_pct <= 0.4 THEN 2 WHEN r_pct <= 0.6 THEN 3 WHEN r_pct <= 0.8 THEN 4 ELSE 5 END AS R_score,
           CASE WHEN f_pct <= 0.2 THEN 1 WHEN f_pct <= 0.4 THEN 2 WHEN f_pct <= 0.6 THEN 3 WHEN f_pct <= 0.8 THEN 4 ELSE 5 END AS F_score,
           CASE WHEN m_pct <= 0.2 THEN 1 WHEN m_pct <= 0.4 THEN 2 WHEN m_pct <= 0.6 THEN 3 WHEN m_pct <= 0.8 THEN 4 ELSE 5 END AS M_score
    FROM percentiles
),
segments AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           CASE WHEN R_score >= 4 AND F_score >= 4 AND M_score >= 4 THEN 'Champions'
                WHEN F_score >= 4 THEN 'Loyal'
                WHEN R_score >= 4 THEN 'Promising'
                WHEN M_score >= 4 THEN 'At Risk'
                ELSE 'Hibernating' END AS segment
    FROM scores
)
SELECT s.segment,
       COUNT(DISTINCT s.CustomerID) AS customers,
       ROUND(SUM(o.TotalDue) / COUNT(o.SalesOrderID), 0) AS aov,
       ROUND(1.0 * COUNT(o.SalesOrderID) / COUNT(DISTINCT s.CustomerID), 2) AS orders_per_customer,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(o.OnlineOrderFlag) / COUNT(o.SalesOrderID), 1) AS online_share_pct
FROM segments s
JOIN ADW_Sales_orders o ON s.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
GROUP BY s.segment

questions.title: Favourite category of each segment
questions.story: Which product category brings the most revenue in each segment? Return the segment, the category, the revenue (LineTotal) and the category's share of the segment's revenue, ranked within each segment. Does any segment buy differently from the others?

approach: The path is segments, ADW_Sales_orders, ADW_Sales_orders_detail, ADW_Dim_Product, ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory and ADW_Dim_ProductCategory.
The product and sub-category ID columns have different data types, so CAST them to the same type before the JOIN.
Bikes are the top category in every segment (77% to 99% of revenue), so the ranking alone says little.
Look at the second place. Champions and Loyal customers buy Components (13.5% and 5.7%), and Hibernating customers buy Accessories (14.9%).

WITH rfm AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           DATEDIFF(day, MAX(OrderDate), '2014-07-01') AS Recency,
           COUNT(DISTINCT SalesOrderID) AS Frequency,
           SUM(TotalDue) AS Monetary
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID

percentiles AS (
    SELECT *,
           PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Recency DESC) AS r_pct,
           PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Frequency) AS f_pct,
           PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Monetary) AS m_pct
    FROM rfm
),
scores AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           CASE WHEN r_pct <= 0.2 THEN 1 WHEN r_pct <= 0.4 THEN 2 WHEN r_pct <= 0.6 THEN 3 WHEN r_pct <= 0.8 THEN 4 ELSE 5 END AS R_score,
           CASE WHEN f_pct <= 0.2 THEN 1 WHEN f_pct <= 0.4 THEN 2 WHEN f_pct <= 0.6 THEN 3 WHEN f_pct <= 0.8 THEN 4 ELSE 5 END AS F_score,
           CASE WHEN m_pct <= 0.2 THEN 1 WHEN m_pct <= 0.4 THEN 2 WHEN m_pct <= 0.6 THEN 3 WHEN m_pct <= 0.8 THEN 4 ELSE 5 END AS M_score
    FROM percentiles
),
segments AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           CASE WHEN R_score >= 4 AND F_score >= 4 AND M_score >= 4 THEN 'Champions'
                WHEN F_score >= 4 THEN 'Loyal'
                WHEN R_score >= 4 THEN 'Promising'
                WHEN M_score >= 4 THEN 'At Risk'
                ELSE 'Hibernating' END AS segment
    FROM scores
),
category_revenue AS (
    SELECT s.segment, pc.ProductCategoryName AS category, SUM(d.LineTotal) AS revenue
    FROM segments s
    JOIN ADW_Sales_orders o ON s.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
    JOIN ADW_Sales_orders_detail d ON o.SalesOrderID = d.SalesOrderID
    JOIN ADW_Dim_Product p ON d.ProductID = p.ProductID
    JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory sc ON CAST(p.ProductSubcategoryID AS VARCHAR) = CAST(sc.ProductSubcategoryID AS VARCHAR)
    JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductCategory pc ON sc.ProductCategoryID = pc.ProductCategoryID
    GROUP BY s.segment, pc.ProductCategoryName
)
SELECT segment, category, ROUND(revenue, 0) AS revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * revenue / SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY segment), 1) AS share_pct,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY segment ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS category_rank
FROM category_revenue
ORDER BY segment, category_rank

questions.title: First purchase month
questions.story: Retention analysis starts by putting each customer in a cohort, which is the month of their first order. For every customer in ADW_Sales_orders, return the CustomerID and the CohortMonth: the first day of the month of the customer's first OrderDate.
questions.hint: MIN(OrderDate) per customer gives the first order. DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(x), MONTH(x), 1) turns a date into the first day of its month.
approach: Everything is in ADW_Sales_orders. Group by CustomerID.
Take MIN(OrderDate), then cut it to the first day of the month.
A cohort is a group that shares a starting point. Here it is the month of the first purchase.
There are 19,119 customers.

steps.sql:
SELECT CustomerID,
       DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(MIN(OrderDate)), MONTH(MIN(OrderDate)), 1) AS CohortMonth
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
GROUP BY CustomerID

questions.title: Cohort sizes
questions.story: How many new customers does each monthly cohort have? Return the CohortMonth and the number of customers.
questions.hint: Use the query from the last question as a CTE, then COUNT(*) grouped by CohortMonth.
approach: Step 1: first order month per customer (the last question) as a CTE.
Step 2: count customers per cohort month.
There are 38 cohorts. Cohorts have about 150 to 350 new customers a month until June 2013, then jump to around 1,000 a month from July 2013 (1,284 in July).

steps.sql:
WITH first_order AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(MIN(OrderDate)), MONTH(MIN(OrderDate)), 1) AS CohortMonth
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID
)
SELECT CohortMonth, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM first_order
GROUP BY CohortMonth

questions.title: Active customers by month since first order
questions.story: For each cohort, count the customers who ordered in each month after their first. Return the CohortMonth, MonthsSinceFirst (0 for the first month) and the number of different active customers.
questions.hint: List the months in which each customer ordered (DISTINCT customer and month), join it to the first order month, and use DATEDIFF(month, cohort month, order month).
approach: Step 1: first order month per customer.
Step 2: the distinct months in which each customer ordered.
Step 3: join steps 1 and 2 and calculate DATEDIFF(month, CohortMonth, OrderMonth). Period 0 is the first month.
Step 4: COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) grouped by cohort and period. Count customers, not orders: a customer with three orders in a month is one retained customer.
485 rows. Only months with at least one active customer appear.

steps.sql:
WITH first_order AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(MIN(OrderDate)), MONTH(MIN(OrderDate)), 1) AS CohortMonth
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID
),
activity AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT CustomerID,
           DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), 1) AS OrderMonth
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
),
cohort_activity AS (
    SELECT f.CohortMonth,
           DATEDIFF(month, f.CohortMonth, a.OrderMonth) AS MonthsSinceFirst,
           a.CustomerID
    FROM first_order f
    JOIN activity a ON f.CustomerID = a.CustomerID
)
SELECT CohortMonth, MonthsSinceFirst, COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) AS active_customers
FROM cohort_activity
GROUP BY CohortMonth, MonthsSinceFirst

questions.title: Cohort table, months 0 to 3
questions.story: Reshape the last result into a cohort table: one row per cohort with four columns, month0, month1, month2 and month3. Each column holds the number of different customers who ordered that many months after their first order.
questions.hint: Conditional aggregation: COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN MonthsSinceFirst = 1 THEN CustomerID END) for each column.
approach: Reuse the cohort_activity CTE from the last question.
One COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN ... END) per month column, grouped by CohortMonth.
A month that has no active customers shows 0 here. For months that have not happened yet, that is misleading, and the next question deals with it.
38 rows, one per cohort.

steps.sql:
WITH first_order AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(MIN(OrderDate)), MONTH(MIN(OrderDate)), 1) AS CohortMonth
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID
),
activity AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT CustomerID,
           DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), 1) AS OrderMonth
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
),
cohort_activity AS (
    SELECT f.CohortMonth,
           DATEDIFF(month, f.CohortMonth, a.OrderMonth) AS MonthsSinceFirst,
           a.CustomerID
    FROM first_order f
    JOIN activity a ON f.CustomerID = a.CustomerID
)
SELECT CohortMonth,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN MonthsSinceFirst = 0 THEN CustomerID END) AS month0,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN MonthsSinceFirst = 1 THEN CustomerID END) AS month1,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN MonthsSinceFirst = 2 THEN CustomerID END) AS month2,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN MonthsSinceFirst = 3 THEN CustomerID END) AS month3
FROM cohort_activity
GROUP BY CohortMonth

questions.title: Retention rates and what they show
questions.story: Add the retention rate to the cohort table. Return the CohortMonth, the cohort size and the retention rate for months 1, 2 and 3 as a percent of the cohort size, rounded to 1 decimal. The data ends on 2014-06-30, so a month that has not happened yet must show NULL, not 0. Then answer: for each cohort, is there anything special?
questions.hint: Retention rate = active customers in that month / cohort size (month0). Show a rate only when the cohort month plus the number of months is on or before 2014-06-01, otherwise leave the CASE without an ELSE.
approach: Reuse the counts from the last question and divide by month0. Multiply by 100.0 to avoid integer division.
An incomplete month looks like zero retention. The 2014-05 cohort cannot have a month 2 yet, so its month 2 must be NULL.
Read across a row to see how one cohort decays, and down a column to see whether newer cohorts retain better.

Findings in this data: the cohort jumps from about 300 to 1,284 customers in July 2013. Newer cohorts return at about 2% to 3% a month. The oldest cohorts rarely return in month 1 or 2 but come back in month 3, which points to a quarterly buying rhythm (for example 83.7% for May 2011).

steps.sql:
WITH first_order AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(MIN(OrderDate)), MONTH(MIN(OrderDate)), 1) AS CohortMonth
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID
),
activity AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT CustomerID,
           DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), 1) AS OrderMonth
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
),
cohort_activity AS (
    SELECT f.CohortMonth,
           DATEDIFF(month, f.CohortMonth, a.OrderMonth) AS MonthsSinceFirst,
           a.CustomerID
    FROM first_order f
    JOIN activity a ON f.CustomerID = a.CustomerID
),
counts AS (
    SELECT CohortMonth,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN MonthsSinceFirst = 0 THEN CustomerID END) AS month0,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN MonthsSinceFirst = 1 THEN CustomerID END) AS month1,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN MonthsSinceFirst = 2 THEN CustomerID END) AS month2,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN MonthsSinceFirst = 3 THEN CustomerID END) AS month3
    FROM cohort_activity
    GROUP BY CohortMonth
)
SELECT CohortMonth,
       month0 AS cohort_size,
       CASE WHEN DATEADD(month, 1, CohortMonth) <= '2014-06-01' THEN ROUND(100.0 * month1 / month0, 1) END AS month1_pct,
       CASE WHEN DATEADD(month, 2, CohortMonth) <= '2014-06-01' THEN ROUND(100.0 * month2 / month0, 1) END AS month2_pct,
       CASE WHEN DATEADD(month, 3, CohortMonth) <= '2014-06-01' THEN ROUND(100.0 * month3 / month0, 1) END AS month3_pct
FROM counts
ORDER BY CohortMonth
